description: We are ASTRAUNI, a team of students from Universidad Nacional de Ingeniería (UNI), Peru, participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We're developing an interactive space mission design game for Challenge 13, combining aerospace engineering, programming, 3D visualization, and simulation. Our goal is to make space exploration more accessible, engaging, and educational through creativity, innovation, and teamwork.
summary: ASTRAUNI presents Mission Architect, a browser-based game that makes spacecraft engineering learnable through experimentation. Players choose a scientific mission, assemble a satellite in 3D, select its orbit and launch option, and balance budget, mass, power and communications. During operations, eclipses, instrument calibration and ground-station interruptions create meaningful choices: keep collecting observations or switch off the camera to protect the battery. Live telemetry and a mission debrief explain why a design succeeds or fails, encouraging players to improve it and try again under reproducible conditions. Eight configurable subsystem categories connect individual components to whole-mission performance. NASA mission-design references and credited Earth and Moon imagery provide educational context, while hardware values and training events are explicitly synthetic. Designed for students and curious beginners, Mission Architect turns abstract engineering trade-offs into visible consequences, addressing the Space Mission Design Game challenge through an accessible design–operate–learn loop.
details:
Mission Architect is an educational browser game developed by ASTRAUNI for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Space Mission Design Game challenge. It helps students understand a central engineering principle: improving one subsystem can create limitations elsewhere in a mission.

THE PLAYER EXPERIENCE

Players progress through five connected stages: mission briefing, spacecraft design, engineering review, operations and debrief. Four scenarios introduce different combinations of scientific data targets, budgets and operational deadlines.

The spacecraft builder offers eight subsystem categories with eight options each: scientific payload, solar generation, batteries, communications, attitude control, onboard computing, thermal systems and propulsion. Components have different mass, cost, electrical demand and modeled capabilities. Supporting systems and selected combinations introduce explicitly synthetic gameplay effects, creating alternative strategies rather than one universally best design.

Players also select orbital altitude, mission duration and a launch option. Engineering review checks constraints such as spacecraft mass and budget and highlights potential power and communication bottlenecks.

DECISIONS WITH VISIBLE CONSEQUENCES

During operations, the numerical engine calculates sunlight and eclipse conditions, battery energy, acquired data and data transmitted during modeled ground contacts. Seeded training events introduce instrument calibration and temporary ground-station unavailability.

In commander mode, the mission pauses at decision points. Players can keep the scientific camera operating or switch it off to reduce electrical demand, sacrificing new observations while preserving energy. An optional comparison shows calculated consequences before issuing an order.

The debrief explains the outcome, identifies limitations and encourages another attempt. Scoring allocates 70 points to returned-data completion, 20 to powered operating time and 10 to unused budget. This score evaluates the educational objective; it is not a probability of real mission success.

VISUALIZATION AND ACCESSIBILITY

A configurable 3D satellite, follow and onboard camera views, an orbital schematic and an educational space explorer make engineering relationships easier to inspect. Spanish and English are available, and a 2D fallback preserves access when 3D graphics are unavailable. Short explanations and component information support beginners without requiring a separate examination.

NASA RESOURCES AND SCIENTIFIC TRANSPARENCY

NASA’s “Design and Develop Science Missions” provides systems-engineering context for connecting objectives, spacecraft, launch, ground operations and evaluation. Credited NASA Blue Marble imagery and NASA Scientific Visualization Studio lunar maps are included as local visual resources.

Our Riverwatch exercise connects the game to the purpose of Earth observation through a fictional flood-observation request. It does not detect floods or estimate humanitarian outcomes.

Hardware specifications, credits, training events and subsystem bonuses are synthetic game parameters. The mission uses an idealized circular Earth-orbit model. Propulsion options do not implement trajectory maneuvers, and displayed spacecraft or debris are not live tracking or collision predictions.

DEVELOPMENT AND INTENDED IMPACT

The project uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber and Vitest, with GitHub collaboration and Cloudflare Pages deployment. Simulation calculations are separated from visualization so graphical changes do not determine engineering results. Automated tests check numerical behavior, reproducibility and interface interactions.

Our intended impact is to make mission design approachable through experimentation: design, operate, understand and improve. The prototype demonstrates this learning approach; its educational effectiveness has not yet been measured through a formal user study.
